# How to learn JavaScript as a complete beginner

:::answer
Learning JavaScript means working through fundamentals in order: variables, functions, arrays and the DOM, then practicing with small projects. Wes Bos offers Beginner JavaScript, a course built for absolute beginners, plus a free 30-day vanilla JS challenge. Start with structured lessons, write code every day, and check your understanding by building something small before moving on.
:::

:::takeaways
- Beginner JavaScript is built specifically for people new to JS or programming entirely.
- JavaScript For Web Designers is a free, exercise-heavy way to learn the basics before committing to a paid course.
- The free 30-day challenge has you build 30 things with no frameworks, compilers or libraries.
- Checking your work by building small, working examples is more useful than reading alone.
- JavaScript fundamentals come before React: Wes Bos also teaches a course bridging the two.

## What do you need before you start?

You need a computer, a text editor, a web browser and time set aside to practice rather than just watch. No prior programming experience is required for the right starting course.

> This is a course for absolute beginners or anyone looking to brush up on their fundamentals. [wesbos.com/courses](https://wesbos.com/courses)

That course is Beginner JavaScript, and the site frames it plainly for newcomers.

> Start here if you are new to JS or programming in general! [wesbos.com/courses](https://wesbos.com/courses)

You don't need to install anything exotic to begin. A browser's developer console and a plain text file are enough for your first exercises, and you can add a code editor once you're writing more than a few lines at a time. What matters more than tooling is consistency, since JavaScript's syntax and quirks sink in through repetition rather than a single read-through.

## What are the steps to learn JavaScript?

Once you have a place to write and run code, the path runs through a beginner course, daily practice, and small projects that force you to apply what you've read.

1. Pick a beginner-level starting point. Wes Bos describes Beginner JavaScript as "a fun, exercise heavy approach to learning Modern JavaScript from scratch," which gives you a structured sequence instead of guessing what to study first. [wesbos.com/courses](https://wesbos.com/courses)
2. Try the free option before committing money. JavaScript For Web Designers is described on the courses page as "A free 25 video course" style resource aimed at people who want the fundamentals without a paid signup first, which lowers the barrier to just starting. [wesbos.com/courses](https://wesbos.com/courses)
3. Work through core syntax: variables, functions, loops, arrays and objects. This is the backbone every later topic, including the DOM and APIs, depends on.
4. Build small, throwaway exercises as you go rather than only watching videos. The exercise-heavy format of the beginner course exists because typing code yourself is what makes it stick.
5. Join a daily-build habit once fundamentals feel steady. The free 30-day vanilla JS coding challenge has you "build 30 things in 30 days with 30 tutorials," using no frameworks, compilers, libraries or boilerplate, which forces plain-JavaScript fluency. [wesbos.com/courses](https://wesbos.com/courses)
6. Move to ES6 once the basics are comfortable. The ES6 course is pitched as the way to learn "all that ES6 has to offer while sharpening your core JavaScript skills," and it assumes you already know core JavaScript going in. [wesbos.com/courses](https://wesbos.com/courses)
7. Only after fundamentals and ES6 are solid, consider a framework. Wes Bos's React course is framed as a step to "upgrade your JavaScript skills to learn React.js in just a couple of afternoons," which only works once the JavaScript underneath it is settled. [wesbos.com/courses](https://wesbos.com/courses)

## How do you check it worked?

You know the fundamentals are sticking when you can write a small working script without copying one, not just when a lesson's example runs. Rebuild a finished exercise from memory a day or two later and see how much you retained.

A useful check is whether you can explain what each line does out loud, to yourself or someone else, without pausing to look it up. If a concept like array methods or function scope still feels shaky, that's the signal to redo that section of the beginner course rather than push ahead. The 30-day challenge works as a check too: if you can finish a day's build without rewatching the matching video, that topic has landed. If you can't, loop back before moving to ES6 or React.

## What mistakes should you avoid?

The most common mistake is skipping fundamentals to jump straight into a framework. Wes Bos's own course order puts Beginner JavaScript and ES6 before React, and the React course assumes those skills are already in place rather than teaching them again.

Another mistake is watching lessons passively instead of typing the exercises yourself. The beginner course is described as exercise heavy for a reason, and skipping the exercises removes the part that builds skill. A third mistake is trying to learn everything in one pass instead of returning to the free 30-day challenge or the beginner course material after a break, since spaced repetition matters more in programming than in most subjects. Finally, avoid chasing every new course that gets announced before finishing the one you're on. Wes Bos notes he's "delivering a few new courses every year," which is useful to know but not a reason to restart your path every time one appears. [wesbos.com/courses](https://wesbos.com/courses)

## How long does it take to learn JavaScript?

There's no fixed number of weeks that applies to everyone, since it depends on how much time you put in and whether you're building projects or only reading. What's clear from the course structure is that it's staged: beginner fundamentals first, then ES6, then frameworks like React, each assuming the previous stage is done.

The free 30-day challenge gives you one concrete pacing option, since it's built around 30 tutorials over 30 days, each producing something you built yourself rather than just watched. [wesbos.com/courses](https://wesbos.com/courses) Treat that as a floor, not a ceiling. Many people spend longer than 30 days on fundamentals alone before they feel ready to move on, and that's normal given how much of JavaScript only clicks through repeated use.

## Should you learn JavaScript before React?

Yes. React sits on top of JavaScript, so weak fundamentals show up immediately once you try to build anything beyond a tutorial copy. Wes Bos's own course lineup reflects this order, with Beginner JavaScript and ES6 listed ahead of the React course.

The React course itself is pitched at people who already have JavaScript skills and want to extend them, described as a way to "upgrade your JavaScript skills to learn React.js in just a couple of afternoons." [wesbos.com/courses](https://wesbos.com/courses) That phrasing assumes an upgrade from something, not a start from zero. Going through Beginner JavaScript and ES6 first means the React-specific concepts, like components and state, are the only new things you're learning instead of fighting JavaScript syntax at the same time.
